A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results from this search yet. Earlier searches ran 84 trials across many families and every one scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success. So the agent never finishes an exact build, and the useful levers are optimisation and inductive bias, not generalisation. One possible cause: the shaping reward pays for filling cells even when a brick also adds extra cells, so a greedy filler earns most of the return without ever building exactly. Nothing tested yet supports any single change. This round tries six stacked candidates that differ a lot from each other. All share orthogonal init, near-uniform starting logits (gain 0.01), GroupNorm, a raw-obs skip into the footprint head, factorised logits (type + anchor + interaction) and a learned global missing-cell detector feeding DONE. They differ in trunk (column MLP, 3x3 residual, dilated, attention), in compute r (about 1 to 2.2) and in recipe (lr 7e-4 to 3e-3, gamma 0.99 to 0.995, lambda 0.9 to 0.99, 1 to 2 epochs). Small minibatches keep the gradient step count high.

### Round 2
Five trials scored 0 on training and dev. r1c6 scored 0.154 on dev and 0.148 on training success. This is the first real signal in any search. Train and dev success are about equal, so generalisation is not the problem; what holds it back is optimisation and the number of samples. Several things set r1c6 apart: a deeper per-column GroupNorm MLP, three residual 3x3 blocks (one dilated), footprint convs plus pooling, small rollouts (128 envs x 16 steps, minibatch 128), 2 epochs and clip 0.25. Gradient-step counts were similar to r1c1, so the trunk and footprint-conv stack may matter, or the result may be seed luck. This round stays close to r1c6. One candidate is a near-copy with a wider column MLP to test luck. Four make one recipe change each: 1 epoch, 3 epochs, gamma 0.995 / lambda 0.97, and lr 2e-3. One stacks the likely recipe gains.

### Round 3
Results are bimodal: a run either breaks through or stays at exactly 0. Only the r1c6 network family has scored above 0. It scored 0.15 with the base recipe (r1c6), 0.34 with 3 epochs (r2c3) and 0.49 with gamma 0.995, lambda 0.97, lr 1.5e-3 and entropy 0.005 (r2c6). The same family scored 0 with a wider column MLP (r2c1), 1 epoch (r2c2), the long horizon alone (r2c4) and lr 2e-3 (r2c5). Training success tracks dev success (0.47 vs 0.49), so these runs are not overfitting. The bottleneck is how often optimisation breaks through. Because of the bimodality, the zeros may be seed luck rather than real harm. What may help: more gradient reuse (3 epochs) and less entropy noise. With two rounds left, I stack r2c6's recipe with 3 epochs, vary entropy, lr and the number of gradient steps, and try one cheap architecture change: a global context broadcast into the placement head. The final score comes from 4 new seeds, so reliability matters.

### Round 4
Only the r1c6 network family has scored above 0 in this search. The recipe drove the gains: 2 epochs scored 0.15, 3 epochs 0.34, gamma 0.995 / lambda 0.97 / lr 1.5e-3 / entropy 0.005 scored 0.49, adding 3 epochs scored 0.67, and full-episode 32-step rollouts scored 0.78. Training success tracks dev success closely (0.70 vs 0.78), so the agent is under-optimised, not overfitting. Seeds are noisy: a near-copy with a wider column MLP (r2c1) scored 0, and so did zero entropy (r3c3). So some runs never break through. 1 epoch and lr 2e-3 under the base recipe both scored 0. In this final round, every candidate stays near r3c6 and changes one thing: 4 epochs, 32 minibatches, lambda 0.99, 48-step rollouts, or a slightly wider head as a near-copy. One candidate stacks the most promising changes. Each aims to raise the chance of breakthrough and push optimisation further.

## Trial it ended with
name: r3c6 + 32 minibatches
hypothesis: Change: n_minibatches 32 (64 samples each) instead of 16, which doubles the gradient steps on the same data.
